newsitem.title: USA: Aradigm drug-delivery system clears hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Aradigm drug-delivery system clears hurdle.

text.p: Aradigm Corp said Friday that a Phase I test of its AERx Pain Management System to use morphine to reduce pain was as effective as morphine delivered intravenously.

The company said data from the two-center clinical trial demonstrated that the speed of onset and the reproducibility of morphine delivery using the AERx system was comparable to morphine delivered intravenously to the same subjects. Blood levels of morphine produced after a single inhalation from the AERx system were consistent with those typically required for pain relief.

The AERx Pain Management System is being designed to provide rapid, safe, patient-controlled relief of pain, at home, to patients suffering from cancer, AIDS, and other chronic severe pain conditions, as well as acute pain following inpatient and outpatient surgeries. Patients may suffer several episodes of severe pain each day -- pain which "breaks through" the baseline level of analgesia provided by available longer-acting products. The AERx Pain Management System will allow patients to treat breakthrough pain without the use of costly, inconvenient intravenous infusion pumps.
Rick Thompson, president of Aradigm said, "Morphine is one of the most important narcotic drugs for the treatment of pain, but for rapid effect it must be delivered intravenously.

The AERx system is achieving the speed of intravenous delivery and should be able to provide rapid relief of breakthrough pain without requiring the use of needles. No other non-invasive drug delivery systems has been shown to deliver morphine this rapidly, efficiently and reproducibly. Our objective is to provide a new approach for the management of severe pain at home."

This two-center clinical trial involved dosing 16 healthy volunteers at Harris Laboratories in Lincoln, Nebraska, and an additional 12 healthy volunteers at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. The last of the planned 28 subjects completed the trial in December. Neither this study nor a pre-clinical safety study raised concerns regarding the safety of delivering morphine via inhalation.

Each year in the U.S., over 1.2 million people are diagnosed with cancer and over 550,000 individuals die of the disease. Over half of all cancer patients suffer from pain, and often this is severe pain which requires the use of narcotic analgesics such as morphine.
